video.title: I Tried OpenClaw for a Month and I'm Never Going Back

summary: Nick describes how he has been learning AI agents and applying them at a large company, where leaders have little experience with the tools. He demonstrates an earnings-call preparation prototype and a personal OpenClaw assistant built around organized, searchable data. He suggests businesses in corporate AI consulting, executive education, data cleanup, custom tools, and meeting follow-up. His central advice is to learn by applying AI to real workplace problems and to keep testing ideas as the technology changes.

speakers.name: Nick
speakers.description: AI-focused guest who describes building and using AI tools at a large company.

ideas.name: Corporate AI adoption consulting
ideas.one_liner: Help companies identify workflow problems and bring practical AI tools into their work.
ideas.business_model: Consulting projects or ongoing advisory; exact model not stated.
ideas.customer: Executives and companies that have not yet learned how to use AI in their work.
ideas.problem: Leaders lack time and familiarity to identify useful AI applications, while work processes contain pain points and missed follow-ups.
ideas.offer: Learn a company's pain points, show leaders practical AI use cases, and help move workflows toward AI-enabled processes.

pricing.notes: Nick discusses consulting and ongoing advisory but gives no specific price for general AI adoption work.

acquisition_channels.details: Nick suggests finding public information about publicly traded companies and their executives, then emailing executives to offer a short update on AI.

quote.text: Cold email every single one of those executives and say, "Hi, I'm Nick. Um, I've been deep into AI in the last year and a half. I know what's coming around the corner and 95% of your competitors don't. I'd love to have five minutes with you so that I can update you on what's coming down the pike."
quote.speaker: Nick

acquisition_channels.details: Nick also suggests cold-calling companies after identifying a customer and distribution channel.

quote.text: If you get educated and you just cold call, literally, you could set up a cloudbot to be like, "Here are all the publicly traded companies because I can go and scrape all of that data."
quote.speaker: Nick

ideas.delivery: Nick describes learning a company's problems, showing practical examples, and implementing AI-enabled workflows. A specific repeatable delivery process is not stated.
unit_economics_claims: Nick says a conversation with an executive team grew from about 15 minutes to five hours as they asked him about AI.
He says AI could save senior executives a day in preparing an earnings-call script.

acquisition.how: Agents can research public company information and draft outreach, but targeted sales still needs human review and meetings. In the UK, cold email to limited companies can be used with appropriate identification and opt-out; sole traders need consent, and cold calls must be screened against TPS/CTPS.

onboarding.how: A human needs to understand the company's workflows, data, and priorities; agents can help collect and organize information.

delivery.how: Agents can build and demonstrate tools, but scoping, implementation choices, and client review require substantial human involvement.

billing.how: Project invoicing or recurring billing could be handled by standard billing software with occasional human checks; no billing workflow is described.

support.how: Client questions and changing requirements need human judgment, though agents can answer routine questions from documented project context.

uk_applicability.notes: The corporate AI adoption gap described could exist in UK companies too. Data protection, confidentiality, and sector-specific requirements would need to be addressed.

risks: The pitch depends on earning trust and demonstrating business value, not just familiarity with AI tools.
Cold outreach must follow UK rules: electronic marketing to sole traders generally needs consent, and cold calling requires TPS/CTPS screening.
Nick's claims about how far behind companies are are based on his experience, not a measured survey.

ideas.name: Earnings-call preparation pipeline
ideas.one_liner: Turn a public company's financial data and past transcripts into a first draft for its next earnings call.
ideas.business_model: Potential software product or service; exact revenue model not stated.
ideas.customer: Publicly traded companies and the executives preparing their quarterly earnings calls.
ideas.problem: Executive teams spend time reviewing data and debating wording for earnings-call scripts.
ideas.offer: An intake and workflow that uses company strategy, past transcripts, and current data to create, workshop, refine, and export an earnings-call draft.

pricing.notes: Nick says he could take the prototype to market but does not state a price.

acquisition_channels.details: Nick showed the prototype to people at his company, who described the time required to prepare for earnings calls and helped surface the opportunity.

quote.text: And so, from this, like I I showed some of the people at my company like, "Hey, this is pretty cool."
quote.speaker: Nick

ideas.delivery: The customer supplies data through an intake workflow. The system creates a first draft, supports a strategy workshop and script refinement, and exports the result. Nick says people still need to review and massage the messaging.
unit_economics_claims: Nick says he spent 12 hours building the prototype.
He estimates that the workflow could give four senior executives 10 hours a year back.

acquisition.how: The transcript only describes an internal demonstration. A repeatable sales channel is not stated; enterprise sales would likely need human-led outreach and trust building.

onboarding.how: A structured intake can collect data and company strategy, while a human checks that the inputs are complete and appropriate.

delivery.how: Software can assemble data and produce drafts, but Nick explicitly says people still need to workshop and refine the messaging.

billing.how: Subscription or project billing could be automated with standard software, though the business's actual billing model is not stated.

support.how: Routine product questions could be handled with documentation and agents; customer-specific reporting needs human review.

uk_applicability.notes: UK public companies also prepare regular financial reports, but the prototype is described around US SEC 10-K and 10-Q filings. It would need UK filing data, reporting practices, and relevant compliance adaptations.

risks: The transcript does not establish that a company has bought or used the prototype.
Financial and executive statements need careful review; an inaccurate draft could create reputational or regulatory problems.
Customer data may be commercially sensitive.

ideas.name: Company data cleanup and organization
ideas.one_liner: Help companies organize inconsistent files and records so AI can find and use them.
ideas.business_model: Project-based data cleanup or implementation service; pricing and contract model not stated.
ideas.customer: Companies with large collections of contracts and other documents stored across inconsistent folders and formats.
ideas.problem: Files are scattered, mislabeled, or stored in different formats, making them hard to retrieve and use in AI workflows.
ideas.offer: Create a clear taxonomy and naming system, categorize files, and prepare the data for reliable search and AI use.

pricing.notes: Nick calls it a potential multi-million-dollar business but does not state a customer price.

ideas.delivery: AI can categorize a large share of files, according to Nick, but a knowledgeable person must decide how to handle ambiguous files and establish the system for querying the data.
unit_economics_claims: Nick estimates AI might categorize files to 80% confidence, with a substantial remainder needing human decisions.

acquisition.how: No acquisition channel is described. Finding and qualifying companies with messy data likely requires targeted research and human sales.

onboarding.how: Agents can inventory files, but the company must define access, sensitivity, and the taxonomy it wants.

delivery.how: Automation can classify much of the corpus, but the transcript says the ambiguous remainder requires experienced human judgment.

billing.how: Project invoicing could be automated with standard tools; no billing method is stated.

support.how: Exceptions, taxonomy changes, and retrieval errors require human review.

uk_applicability.notes: The underlying problem is common to organizations in the UK. Handling personal or confidential records would need suitable data protection, security, and access controls.

risks: Automated classification can misfile ambiguous documents.
The service may require substantial manual work for exceptions and taxonomy decisions.
Access to contracts and internal records creates confidentiality and data protection obligations.

quotes.text: So that would be like the first thing I would say is just helping companies get clean data is a multi-million dollar business.

tactics.name: Learn company problems from inside the organization
steps: Consider working at a company to see how its teams operate.
Notice where employees struggle, where spreadsheets are used, and where work slips through the cracks.
Use those observed pain points to identify possible AI services or tools.

quote.text: If you're on a meeting that could have been an email, that's an opportunity. If somebody let something slip through the cracks, that's an opportunity.
quote.speaker: Nick

tactics.name: Use a short AI update to open executive conversations
steps: Identify publicly traded companies and find executive contact information from public sources.
Write a concise, relevant message that offers a short briefing on practical AI changes.
Expect rejection and improve the pitch based on responses.
Use the first meeting to demonstrate a concrete workflow rather than just describe AI.

quote.text: If you can get on their calendar and just have like what I had with that executive team, like within a couple of minutes, they're going to be like, "Oh, I get it. I get it."
quote.speaker: Nick

tactics.name: Treat an AI demo as a prototype, not proof of demand
steps: Build a small demo around one real workflow.
Show it to people who do that work and ask what the process currently costs them.
Use their feedback to decide whether to refine, sell, or abandon the idea.

quote.text: And so, from this, like I I showed some of the people at my company like, "Hey, this is pretty cool."
quote.speaker: Nick

tactics.name: Keep a human review stage in AI-generated earnings scripts
steps: Collect the company strategy and current reporting data.
Generate an initial draft from prior transcripts and the new data.
Workshop the recommendations, refine the script, and export only after people review it.

quote.text: The thing that people miss here is they think AI just does everything. It doesn't. It's a good help but like you still have to work shop things.
quote.speaker: Nick

tactics.name: Create a clear taxonomy before building AI retrieval
steps: Inventory where files are stored and identify inconsistent folder and naming conventions.
Agree on a hierarchy and common naming structure.
Use AI to categorize files, then have an experienced person resolve ambiguous cases.
Prepare the resulting data for search and retrieval.

quote.text: Now, clean data would be clear taxonomy, which a taxonomy would just be a hierarchical way for you to to uh identify information.
quote.speaker: Nick

tactics.name: Start with meeting capture and follow-up
steps: Record meetings with appropriate participant notice.
Transcribe and summarize the meeting.
Save the transcript and summary in a searchable location.
Extract commitments and create reminders for agreed follow-up.

quote.text: But if you just record meetings, document what was said, and then put it in a place where you can go and get back to later or build something that reminds you
quote.speaker: Nick

tactics.name: Use multiple models to review plans and specifications
steps: Ask one model to turn an idea into a product requirements document.
Send the document to other models for an adversarial review.
Revise the specification through several review rounds.
Repeat the review for the implementation plan before building.

quote.text: And I go through like four rounds of that. And after those four rounds, I've got something that's pretty good.
quote.speaker: Nick

tactics.name: Test a physical product idea where customers already are
steps: Take the printer to school and offer on-demand printing.
Try specific products such as team shirts, customized spikes, tumblers, phone cases, and stickers.
Ask which products and colors customers prefer and what they will pay.
Follow customer demand instead of committing early to one product.

quote.text: How much will people pay? What colors do they like? Do they want tumblers? Do they want their phone cases engraved? Stickers, whatever.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use new technology for rapid testing
steps: Treat a new tool as a way to test many possible offers.
Run small experiments and observe actual demand.
Keep options open until customers show where interest is strongest.

quote.text: That's what you should do with this. And leave your options open and then just chase the energy.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner
